entry: [[Zen]] Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan, officially named Rokuon-ji and nicknamed after its Golden Pavilion (*Kinkaku*). The three-story pavilion, which houses relics of the Buddha, has its top two floors covered in gold leaf. The site was a villa bought in 1397 by the [[Shogun|shōgun]] Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, who had it transformed into a temple complex. After his death his son converted it into a Zen temple, according to his wishes. In 1950 a 22-year-old novice monk burned the original pavilion, which was rebuilt in 1955 and is said to be a close copy. The temple is a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]]. [[Yukio Mishima]]'s 1956 book *The Temple of the Golden Pavilion* fictionalized the arson.

Group of islands and county of the Republic of China ([[Taiwan]]), 10 km (6 mi) east of [[Xiamen]] in Fujian, China. Kinmen, also called Quemoy, lies 187 km (116 mi) west of the main island of Taiwan across the [[Taiwan Strait]]. Its strategic location has caused repeated confrontations. In August 1958 the [[People's Liberation Army]] heavily bombarded the islands during the Second Taiwan Strait Crisis. Travel restrictions to the main island of Taiwan were lifted in 1994, and a ferry route to Xiamen opened in January 2001.

Capital and largest city of the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]], on the southern shore of the [[Congo River]] at Pool Malebo, opposite [[Brazzaville]], capital of the [[Republic of the Congo]]. The two cities are separated by a four-kilometer-wide span of the river and form the world's closest pair of capital cities. Kinshasa is the country's leading economic, political and cultural center, with manufacturing, telecommunications, banking and entertainment industries. Named Léopoldville by Henry Morton Stanley for [[Leopold II of Belgium]], it was renamed Kinshasa in 1966 during [[Mobutu Sese Seko]]'s Zairianization campaign. French is the language of government and high-end commerce, while Lingala serves as the [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] of the street. It is the largest nominally Francophone urban area in the world.

Web of social relationships based on descent and marriage, central to human societies. In anthropology, kinship refers both to these relationships and to the study of them. Ties through descent are distinguished from [[Affinity (law)|affinity]], the ties created by marriage. Kinship organizes people into social groups, roles and [[Genealogy|genealogies]]. Anthropologist Robin Fox argued that humans work with the same basic facts of life as animals, such as mating, gestation and parenthood, but conceptualize them to serve social ends. These ends include the [[Socialization|socialization]] of children and the formation of economic, political and religious groups. In biology, kinship denotes the degree of genetic relatedness between individuals, as in kin selection theory. Many ethical codes treat obligations among kin as stronger than those owed to strangers, as in Confucian filial piety.

Two equalities describing current and potential difference (commonly known as [[Voltage|voltage]]) in electrical circuits. First described in 1845 by German physicist [[Gustav Kirchhoff]], the laws generalized the work of [[Georg Ohm]] and preceded that of [[James Clerk Maxwell]]. The current law states that the algebraic sum of currents at any node (junction) is zero. The voltage law states that the directed sum of potential differences around any closed loop is zero. Both can be understood as corollaries of [[Maxwell's equations]] in the low-frequency limit. They are accurate for direct-current (DC) circuits and for alternating-current circuits at frequencies whose wavelengths are very large compared with the circuit. A matrix version of the current law is the basis of most circuit simulation software, such as SPICE. The laws do not apply where the lumped-element model fails, as in high-frequency AC circuits.

Island country in the central [[Pacific Ocean]], spanning the [[Micronesia|Micronesia]] and [[Polynesia|Polynesia]] sub-regions of Oceania. Its islands straddle the [[Equator]] and the 180th meridian, and its easternmost islands lie in the most advanced time zone on Earth, UTC+14. Its total land area is 811 sq km (313 sq mi). Britain made the Gilbert Islands a protectorate in 1892, and Kiribati became independent from the [[United Kingdom]] in 1979. The permanent population is just over 138,000 as of the 2026 census, and more than half live on Tarawa, the capital. The country once exported phosphate from Banaba, but that mine is virtually exhausted. Fisheries, subsistence agriculture and copra drive much of the economy, and the government relies heavily on fishing license fees and foreign aid. Kiribati joined the [[United Nations]] in 1999. As a low-lying atoll nation it is highly vulnerable to sea-level rise and [[Climate change|climate change]].

American actor and producer. He made his film debut in *The Strange Love of Martha Ivers* (1946) and became a leading box-office star in the 1950s, appearing in dramas, westerns and war films. Academy Award nominations for *Champion* (1949), *The Bad and the Beautiful* (1952) and *Lust for Life* (1956) recognized his work, the last as [[Vincent van Gogh]]. Douglas worked with director [[Stanley Kubrick]] on *Paths of Glory* and *Spartacus*. His production company, Bryna Productions, gave screenwriter Dalton Trumbo an on-screen credit for *Spartacus*, a step credited with helping to break the Hollywood blacklist. In 1963 he starred in the Broadway play *One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest*, a story he later gave to his son [[Michael Douglas]], who made it into an Oscar-winning film.

Indian playback singer and actor. Kumar was one of the most popular singers in the [[Indian subcontinent]] and one of the most influential in Indian music. Known for yodeling and for singing in different voices, he sang in many Indian languages, including [[Hindi]], Bengali, Marathi and Malayalam. He won eight Filmfare Awards for Best Male Playback Singer, a record for the category. The Madhya Pradesh government gave him its Lata Mangeshkar Award in 1985, and in 1997 it created the Kishore Kumar Award for contributions to Hindi cinema.

American rock band formed in [[New York City]] in 1973, known for face paint, costumes and pyrotechnic stage shows. The original members were Paul Stanley, Gene Simmons, Ace Frehley and Peter Criss. After commercial decline in the early 1980s, the band revived its popularity in 1983 by performing without makeup. Its album *Lick It Up* and its videos on [[MTV]] introduced it to a new generation of fans. The original lineup reunited in 1996, and the band retired after its final show in December 2023. Its four original members were inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2014. Kiss has earned 30 gold albums, the most of any American band.

Touching or pressing of the lips against another person, animal or object. Kissing can express love, passion, affection, respect, a wish for peace or good luck, and other meanings that vary widely between cultures. In some situations it serves as a greeting, a ritual or a symbolic gesture of religious devotion or institutional respect. Biologically, kissing triggers the release of hormones such as [[Oxytocin|oxytocin]], which foster bonding and attachment. Romantic or sexual kissing is not universal: a cross-cultural study found it in only about 46% of 168 societies surveyed. Kissing is recorded in texts from [[Mesopotamia]] dating back at least to 2500 BCE, where it appeared in both ritual and intimate contexts.

Room or area in a dwelling or commercial establishment used for cooking and food preparation. A modern middle-class residential kitchen typically has a stove, a sink with hot and cold running water, a [[Refrigerator|refrigerator]], and modular cabinets and worktops. Many households also have a [[Microwave oven|microwave oven]] and a [[Dishwasher|dishwasher]]. The main functions are to store, prepare and cook food and to wash dishes, and the room may also be used for dining, entertaining and [[Laundry|laundry]]. Commercial kitchens in [[Restaurant|restaurants]], [[Hospital|hospitals]] and army barracks are larger and use heavier equipment. In developed countries they are inspected periodically by public-health officials and are forced to close if they fail hygiene requirements. Many modern layouts follow the work triangle principle, which places the sink, stove and refrigerator to minimize movement.

Tethered heavier-than-air craft with wing surfaces that create lift and drag in the wind. Lift results from low pressure above and high pressure below the wings, and the resulting force is opposed by the tension of one or more tethers. The anchor may be fixed or moving, as when a kite is towed by a running person or boat. Kites can also be used in underwater currents on the same principles. Man-lifting kites were used for reconnaissance and during the development of the first practical [[Aircraft|aircraft]], the biplane. Kites are flown for recreation, art and festivals, and sport kites perform aerial ballet. Power kites are multi-line steerable kites that generate large forces for kite surfing and snow kiting.

Fox or fox spirit in Japanese folklore, with the supernatural ability to shapeshift or bewitch other life forms. In [[Shinto]] tradition, kitsune serve as messengers of Inari, the deity of rice and agriculture. The number of a kitsune's tails signifies its age and power. Benevolent zenko are aligned with Inari and bring good fortune, while malevolent yako, or nogitsune, are known for illusions, possession and pranks. Kitsune appear in religious rituals, literature and modern media, where they symbolize transformation and the blurred line between human and divine.

Juvenile [[Cat|cat]]. Kittens are born altricial and are fully dependent on their mothers for survival. They normally do not open their eyes for seven to ten days. After about two weeks they develop quickly and begin to explore beyond the nest. After a further three to four weeks they begin to eat solid food and grow baby teeth. Domestic kittens are highly social animals and usually enjoy human companionship.

Flightless bird endemic to [[New Zealand]], in the order Apterygiformes. The five extant species belong to the genus *Apteryx*. Approximately the size of a domestic [[Chicken|chicken]], kiwi are the smallest ratites. DNA sequence comparisons show they are more closely related to the extinct Malagasy [[Elephant bird|elephant birds]] than to the [[Moa|moa]] that shared New Zealand with them. Four of the five species are listed as vulnerable and one as near threatened. Predation by invasive mammals is the greatest current threat. The vestigial wings are hidden beneath hair-like feathers. Kiwi eggs are among the largest in proportion to body size of any bird, up to 20% of the female's weight. The kiwi is an icon of New Zealand, and the term is used internationally as the colloquial name for New Zealanders.

Edible berry produced by several species of woody vines in the genus *Actinidia*, also called Chinese gooseberry. The most common cultivar group, "Hayward", is oval, about the size of a large hen's egg, with fuzzy light brown skin and light green or golden flesh containing tiny edible black seeds. The fruit is native to central and eastern China, and its first recorded description dates to the 12th century, during the [[Song dynasty]]. Cultivation spread to [[New Zealand]] in the early 20th century, where the first commercial plantings took place. It gained popularity among British and American servicemen stationed there during [[World War II]], and it was exported to the United Kingdom and Australia from 1953 and to [[California]] from 1959. As of 2023, China produced 55% of the world's kiwifruit, making it the largest global producer.

German [[Schutzstaffel|SS]] officer and war criminal, known as the "Butcher of Lyon." As head of the [[Gestapo]] in [[Lyon]] during World War II, he personally tortured prisoners, primarily [[Jews]] and members of the French Resistance. After the war, United States intelligence services employed him for his anti-communist work and aided his escape to [[Bolivia]], where he advised the government on repressing opposition. In 1983 he was extradited to France, convicted of crimes against humanity and sentenced to life in prison. He died of cancer in his Lyon prison cell.

German actor known for intense, volatile performances. Kinski appeared in more than 130 films over a career spanning 41 years. He is best known for five films directed by [[Werner Herzog]], including *Aguirre, the Wrath of God*, *Nosferatu the Vampyre* and *Fitzcarraldo*, a relationship Herzog chronicled in the documentary *My Best Fiend*. His roles ranged across spaghetti Westerns and [[Horror film|horror films]]. His eccentric projects included a one-man show about [[Jesus]] and a biopic of [[Niccolò Paganini]] that he directed and starred in. His notoriety has produced a widespread cult following.

Austrian statesman and diplomat who stood at the center of the European balance of power for three decades. He served as Austrian foreign minister from 1809 and as chancellor from 1821 until the [[Revolutions of 1848]] forced his resignation. He engineered a détente with [[Napoleon]] that included Napoleon's marriage to the Austrian archduchess Marie Louise, then Austria's entry into the War of the Sixth Coalition on the Allied side, and the Treaty of Fontainebleau that sent Napoleon into exile. As Austria's delegate at the [[Congress of Vienna]], he helped divide post-Napoleonic Europe among the major powers. He was given the title of Prince in October 1813. Under his guidance an international system of congresses continued for another decade, after which his influence declined.

Person granted an honorary title of knighthood for service to a monarch, church or country, especially in a military capacity. The concept may have been inspired by the ancient Greek hippeis and the Roman equites. In the Early Middle Ages in Western Christian Europe, knighthood was conferred on mounted warriors, and in the High Middle Ages it was considered a class of petty [[Nobility|nobility]]. Often a knight was a vassal who served a lord as an elite fighter, paid with land. By the Late Middle Ages the rank was associated with [[Chivalry|chivalry]], a code of conduct for the courtly Christian warrior. The [[Crusades]] brought military orders of knights to the forefront of defending Christian pilgrims in the Holy Land. New weapons such as the culverin made armored knights obsolete, but the titles remained in many countries.

Catholic military order, formally the Order of Knights of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem. It grew out of a hospital in Jerusalem, founded by merchants from Amalfi to care for pilgrims, and Pope Paschal II recognized it as a distinct order in 1113. The order fought in the [[Crusades]] until the Siege of Acre in 1291. It was then based at [[Rhodes]], over which it was sovereign (1310–1522), and later at [[Malta]] (1530–1798). The Hospitallers also held the North African city of Tripoli for two decades in the 16th century.

Catholic military order founded in 1118 to defend pilgrims on their way to [[Jerusalem]], with its headquarters on the Temple Mount. Officially called the Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon, the order was endorsed by the [[Catholic Church]] and became a favored charity throughout Christendom. Its knights, in white mantles with red crosses, were among the most skilled fighting units of the [[Crusades]]. Non-combatant members, who made up as much as 90% of the order, ran an economic network with early forms of banking and nearly 1,000 commanderies and fortifications across Europe and the Holy Land. In 1307 [[Philip IV of France]] had many of the order's members in France arrested; many were tortured into giving false confessions and burned at the stake. Under pressure from Philip, Pope Clement V disbanded the order in 1312. Between 1317 and 1319 some Templar knights, properties and assets were absorbed by the Portuguese Order of Christ and the Spanish Order of Montesa.

Method of forming fabric by interlooping a continuous length of [[Yarn|yarn]] into rows of connected loops. Hand knitting creates loops one at a time with straight or circular needles. Machine knitting forms loops on hooks that work an entire row at a time. Differences in yarn fiber and weight, needle size and stitch type yield fabrics with different texture, thickness, heat retention and water resistance. A small sample of knitwork, called a swatch, helps the maker determine the gauge of the intended work. Knitting differs from [[Weaving|weaving]], which interlaces yarns at right angles.

Archaeological site and ancient urban center in [[Crete]], Greece, on the southern edge of Heraklion. Settlement on Kephala hill began around 7000 BC, and Knossos became the largest and best-known center of the [[Minoan civilization]]. It is widely considered Europe's oldest city. Its central monument is the Palace of Minos, first built around 1900 BC and rebuilt after a major destruction around 1700 BC. A palatial destruction is conventionally dated to about 1350 BC, although the chronology remains debated. Knossos is closely associated with Greek myths including the [[Minotaur|Minotaur]], and the palace's complex plan was remembered in later Greek tradition as the Labyrinth. In 2025 Knossos was inscribed as part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Minoan Palatial Centres.

Intentional complication in cordage, which may be practical, decorative or both. Practical knots are classified by function: hitches fasten a rope to another object, bends fasten two ends of a rope to each other, loop knots form a loop, and splices are multi-strand knots. In the strictest sense a knot can also be a stopper at the end of a rope that keeps it from slipping through an eye. Knots have interested people since ancient times for their practical uses and their [[Topology|topological]] intricacy, which is studied in [[Knot theory|knot theory]]. In mathematics a knot is a closed curve in three-dimensional space, without self-intersections, considered up to continuous deformation.
